messages.author: a08a2def4527ebe2
messages.subject: CDF of bivariate normal
parts:
Hello everyone, 

I would like to estimimate a two-dimensional ordinal probit, where the link function is based on the CDF of a bivariate normal. This function is currently not implemented in Stan. 

Noah Silbert has a neat trick on his blog, where he use a large, precomputed matrix of the CDF of a bivariate normal, and then use trilinear interpolation within WinBugs to find the appropriate CDF-values.

Does any of you know if the interpolation method can be used in Stan? (or a better idea for implementing the bivariate CDF in current version of Stan...)

Ole-Petter

messages.author: 8aa9b8cc06fdc99c
messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] CDF of bivariate normal
parts:
Stan needs gradients. So if you can code it up
so that the gradients work out, then that should work.

Or you could code up a numerical algorithm (as a Stan
function) and hope that autodiffing through that works
well enough in the range in which your parameters lie.

As you saw, we don't have anything built in.

- Bob

messages.author: a08a2def4527ebe2
messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] CDF of bivariate normal
parts:
I'd just like to add an epilogue here. It seems that Bayesian analysis if these bivariate normals are tricky..according to Greene in the "Modeling Ordered Choices" book, MCMC-estimators are around 25 times slower than alternatives. 

I coded up an ML-estimator of a bivariate, ordinal probit based on the mvtnorm package in R. Works great and is pretty fast.

If ever the CDF of bivariate Normal ends up in Stan I would very much like to give it a go. But for now it seems ML is better. 

-op

Just a friendly reminder that “fast” != “robust inference”.  When something
is a lot slower in full Bayes its almost always an indication that ML isn’t
capturing anywhere near the full uncertainty in the model.

messages.author: 8aa9b8cc06fdc99c
messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] CDF of bivariate normal
parts:
How do you evaluate "works great"?

MCMC algorithms differ from each other by orders of
magnitude in terms of time per effective draw and often
you don't need nearly as much precision in an estimate
as people use for comparison (each additional decimal place of
accuracy is a factor of 100 in additional run time [after
warmup] for MCMC). So evaluation is tricky.

- Bob
